lesson_title: Three Kitchens: Free Market, Central Plan, and the Mix We Actually Live In
hook_text: One school. Three kitchens. Three completely different answers to who eats.
clip_script: One school, one set of hungry learners, three questions that have to be answered before anyone eats. What do we cook? How do we cook it? And who gets a plate? Kitchen one is the tuckshop. Nobody is in charge. Vetkoek sell out by nine, pies go stale, so tomorrow there are more vetkoek. Nobody sent a memo — the till did the talking. Learners with money eat well. Learners without money watch. That's the free market. Kitchen two is the feeding scheme. One official sets the menu for the whole term, one budget, one recipe, everybody gets a plate whether they have money or not. Nobody goes hungry. But if the menu says samp on Tuesdays and everybody hates samp, you eat samp all term, because there's no till to tell anyone otherwise. That's central planning: fairer plates, worse information. And here's the thing — a price is a message. Sold out by nine means people want more. A planning office has no till, so it has to guess for forty million people. But the till has one cruel habit: it only hears money. A hungry learner with no coins sends no message at all. Which is exactly why almost every real school runs a feeding scheme AND a tuckshop. That's a mixed economy. That's South Africa.
visual_style: Split-screen school kitchens: a busy tuckshop counter with a chalkboard price list, a steel serving line with identical trays, then the two merging into one wide shot of a schoolyard at break.
mood: Familiar and playful, landing on something genuinely serious.
pacing: Three quick kitchen beats, a slower reflective middle on prices as messages, decisive close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and classify any economy in the world in three sentences.
